verdicts.rewritten_summary: BBC (12 May 2021): Douala court jailed trans woman Shakiro (YouTuber) and friend Patricia for five years under 'attempted homosexuality' plus 200,000 CFA francs ($370) each — the maximum statutory term — with appeal filed; detained since February 2021. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called it a political decision with no proof of acts. Notes Cameroon's 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, one of 31 African countries criminalising, with beatings of gay/trans people common in public.
verdicts.note: freshness confirmed 2026-08-24: criminalisation and aggressive prosecution unchanged

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Wikipedia biography of Shakiro (b. 29 July 1997, Douala): Cameroonian trans activist who gained Facebook/YouTube following discussing trans life; arrested and charged with 'attempted homosexuality' in 2021, sentenced to five years, subsequently fled Cameroon and claimed asylum abroad. Serves as biographical corroboration of the 2021 case and its outcome (exile), tracking the human-rights profile of the criminalisation cases.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Human Rights Watch (11 May 2022): documented a 2022 uptick of violence against LGBTI people — since 9 March, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least 6 and detained 11 people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; gendarmes beat two in detention. Frames the pattern: the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence, per HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi.

CNN (9 Jan 2013): Cameroon appeals court acquitted Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome, jailed five years in November 2011 solely because they wore women's clothes and ordered Baileys — the original judge had cited dress, speech and the drink as proof they were gay. Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts (lawyer Alice Nkom, All Out petition; Amnesty welcomed the acquittal). Establishes the pattern: arrests on effeminacy/appearance grounds under colonial-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: EUAA COI Query Response Q29 (May 2024) on the Republic of the Congo: systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by state and society, and availability of state protection for LGBTQI+ people. Key findings: no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults; Penal Code Article 331 (per ILGA) sets age of consent at 21 for same-sex vs 18 for different-sex acts; the under-21 'shameless act / against nature' provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is 'ambiguous', and sources say it is used to justify discrimination.
verdicts.note: cached PDF corrupt; body recovered by refetch

verdicts.rewritten_summary: US State Department 2022 human rights report (Republic of the Congo), SOGI section: no law specifically prohibits consensual same-sex conduct between adults; a provision punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under age 21 (6 months–3 years plus fine), scope ambiguous and not invoked for prosecutions. Police at times cite the provision to extract bribes from gay men; local NGOs reported violence, psychological/physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by government and nonstate actors.

US State Department 2023 human rights report (Republic of the Congo): no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguous under-21 provision during 2023; police continued using the 'act against nature' law as a pretext to solicit bribes from men; NGOs reported continuing psychological/physical harassment and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government actors and nonstate actors, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.
verdicts.note: freshness confirmed 2026-08-05: legalised in 2005 penal code, no protections, discrimination documented — unchanged

verdicts.rewritten_summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.
verdicts.note: outcome source: this is the decriminalisation event

verdicts.rewritten_summary: PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

El País (14 Apr 2025): the transphobic murder of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello (Antioquia, near Medellín) — a 28-second video, viral since 5 April, shows her flailing in a creek unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands before drowning; her mother Sandra Borja: 'They killed her for being who she was.' President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities; the report notes 13 trans people killed in Q1 2025.

CNN (6 Aug 2025): killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case — in Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals ('All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans'); describes Millerey's limbs broken before she was pushed into churning water outside Medellín, and frames the repeated killings of LGBTQ people as calculated brutality even amid the country's decades-long civil war.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: The Guardian (30 Jul 2024): more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023, and armed groups threaten a further wave of 'social cleansing' in Caquetá — flyer campaigns announce cleansing of 'drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots'. Trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men; trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work; a friend of interviewee Yesenia Rodríguez was killed.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): strong formal protections (marriage since 2016, adoption since 2015, ID change without medical exams) versus documented killing — the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025. July 2023: the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution (a crime against humanity); UN Human Rights Committee noted concern.
verdicts.note: freshness confirmed 2026-09-21: progressive regime (marriage/adoption/detainee protections) still stands

verdicts.rewritten_summary: JURIST (May 2025): UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination Graeme Reid concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities — praised the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality, but warned of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience: widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT individuals must be urgently addressed as killings rise.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: International Business Times (June 2015): Colombia approved a rule change letting trans people change the sex marker on government-issued ID by signing a document before a notary, replacing the old route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric exams — official Reyes called those exams 'profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice'.

Human Rights Watch (4 Dec 2017): 120+ interviews (incl. nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials, 21 M23 fighters) document security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda/Rwanda in Oct–Dec 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi — background on state violence and impunity in the security environment; no LGBT-specific content.

Queer In The World (updated 3 Dec 2023; covers both Congos): DRC-specific parts — homosexuality legal but LGBT expression censored with imprisonment exposure; violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people reported involving police, security forces and army; no legal gender change for trans people; advises visitors discretion and low profile.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report (Comoros): same-sex conduct criminalised under the penal code, but authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law; no non-discrimination law; police reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons and none was reported that year; widespread impunity listed among major human-rights problems. (Corrects the old claim: the Dec 2024 couple conviction is not in this 2023 report — it comes from the 2024 Outright/Blade sources.)

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Art. 300 of the 2020 penal code punishes same-sex acts with 6 months–2 years plus a 100,000–300,000 franc (US$240–720) fine; no discrimination protections, no legal gender-marker change, no known LGBTIQ organisations (Art. 5 of Law 86-006/AF chills registration); enforcement documented — first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy after a leaked video (2022), first same-sex arrests of two women June 2024, conviction Dec 2024 with time served; government repeatedly refused UN decriminalisation recommendations.

Washington Blade (23 Dec 2024): Comoros court on 12 Dec 2024 sentenced two lesbian women to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served — the couple had been arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them; first conviction of this kind, called a human-rights violation by Human Dignity Trust; article cites Art. 318 (up to five years) as the provision.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised; employment discrimination protection covers sexual orientation (not gender identity); no same-sex union recognition; LGBTIQ orgs register freely; first public Pride 2013 (second African country); 2019–21 polls: 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour; Cabo Verde one of two African UN LGBTI Core Group members, made 2024 UPR anti-discrimination commitments.

Equal Eyes (20 Jul 2018): 2018 Pride Week in Praia — parade plus NGO campaigns (Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, Associação LGBTI de Praia, Associação Arco Iris) petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged.

Observador/Lusa (11 Jul 2017): PM Ulisses Correia e Silva said same-sex marriage is not on the government's agenda, distancing himself from MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro's opposition, after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Rede Angola interview (22 Jun 2016) with Tchinda Andrade, first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde (came out 1997, age 19): describes Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reports verbal violence and two physical attacks; civil law blocked her legal change to a female name — no legal gender recognition as of 2016.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct legal since 1971; first Central American country to adopt marriage equality (2020); since 2018 (Executive Decree 41173-MP) legal gender change on documents without surgery or court order; state health system funds gender-affirming care; rollback pressure — conversion-therapy bill stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.

GayLawNet Costa Rica legal reference: survivor's pension extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (Ministry of Labor announcement 25 Jun 2016; individual survivor benefit approved 29 Jun 2018; teachers' separate budget excluded); also records the 2000 Supreme Court ruling that IVF is unconstitutional — dated partnership-benefits context.

PinkNews (1 May 2008): the Costa Rican government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia (17 May); President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate, promote and support activities 'directed at the eradication of homophobia' — credit to LGBT group CIPAC.

The Tico Times (16 May 2014): President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May (officially recognised since 2008); lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties called it a 'provocation' while a same-sex civil union bill was pending — organised political opposition alongside official recognition.
